notes.front: What is rigidity in space?
notes.back: A spinning gyro’s tendency to resist tilting or turning in any direction other than around its spin axis.
notes.explanation: The handbook names rigidity and precession as the two gyro characteristics that gyroscopic instrument systems use for flight without a visible horizon.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Gyroscopic Systems”, PDF p. 111
notes.evidence: wheel is spun at high speed, it becomes rigid and resists tilting
notes.example: Like a spinning top that stays upright while you tilt the table under it, but mounted in gimbals inside an instrument case.

notes.front: What is a turn-and-slip indicator?
notes.back: A gyro rate instrument whose needle shows the rate of turn (yaw about the vertical axis), with an inclinometer ball beneath it.
notes.explanation: Its gyro is spun by air or an electric motor and deflects the needle through precession when the aircraft yaws.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Gyroscopic Instruments”, PDF p. 116
notes.evidence: When the aircraft yaws, or rotates about its vertical axis, it produces a force in the horizontal plane that, due to precession,
notes.example: Like a car gauge that shows how fast the heading is swinging round, not how far the car is leaning.

notes.front: What is the inclinometer?
notes.back: The ball sealed in a curved, liquid-filled glass tube below a turn indicator; it shows whether a turn is coordinated.
notes.explanation: The ball weighs the force of gravity against the inertia of the turn, so its position shows how the two compare.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Gyroscopic Instruments”, PDF p. 115
notes.evidence: The inclinometer in the instrument is a black glass ball sealed inside a curved glass tube that is partially filled with a liquid
notes.example: Like a marble in a curved spirit level on a car dashboard, which rolls to one side when the car corners too fast for the road’s camber.

notes.front: What is an air data computer (ADC)?
notes.back: A computer that takes pitot pressure, static pressure and temperature and calculates altitude, IAS, TAS and air temperature.
notes.explanation: It sends these values in digital form to other aircraft systems, including electronic flight displays.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Flight Support Systems”, PDF p. 118
notes.evidence: pressure, and temperature to calculate very precise altitude, IAS, TAS, and air temperature.
notes.example: Like a weather station that turns raw pressure and temperature readings into numbers people can use, but its outputs are altitude and airspeed for the flight displays.

notes.front: What is a multi-function display (MFD)?
notes.back: A flight-deck screen beside the PFD that shows information in addition to the primary flight information.
notes.explanation: The PFD in front of the pilot keeps the flight instruments; the MFD carries the extra pictures, such as maps.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Electronic Flight Instrument Systems”, PDF p. 123
notes.evidence: In addition to a PFD directly in front of the pilot, an MFD that provides the display of information in addition to primary flight information is used within the flight deck.
notes.example: Like a second monitor next to a laptop: the main screen keeps the essential work and the side one holds reference pages.

notes.front: What are PFD trend indicators?
notes.back: Coloured trend lines on a PFD’s airspeed and altitude tapes and turn-rate indicator showing where each value is heading.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls the trend vector one of the improvements glass displays brought to general aviation.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying”, “Trend Indicators”, PDF p. 159
notes.evidence: general aviation industry is the trend vector. Trend vectors are colored lines that appear on the airspeed and altitude indicator
notes.example: Like the dotted line a weather app draws ahead of a storm, showing where it will be shortly if nothing changes.

notes.front: In an AHRS, what is a magnetometer?
notes.back: The sensor that measures the Earth’s magnetic field; with inertial sensors and rate gyros, it is one of the solid-state parts of an AHRS.
notes.explanation: Today’s small AHRS units combine several solid-state sensors, and the magnetometer is the magnetic one among them.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Flight Support Systems”, PDF p. 117
notes.evidence: solid-state systems integrating a variety of technology such as low cost inertial sensors, rate gyros, and magnetometers,
notes.example: Like the compass chip in a smartphone that turns the map to face the way you are walking.

notes.front: What is a horizontal situation indicator (HSI)?
notes.back: A heading instrument that combines the magnetic compass with navigation signals and a glideslope in one display.
notes.explanation: Its compass card is driven by a flux valve, and the course and glideslope information sit on top of it.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Horizontal Situation Indicator (HSI)”, PDF p. 118
notes.evidence: This instrument, shown in Figure 5-38, combines the magnetic compass with navigation signals and a glideslope.
notes.example: Like a car satnav that puts the compass, the planned route and your offset from it on one screen.

notes.front: What is a radio magnetic indicator (RMI)?
notes.back: An indicator with a compass card that turns automatically with heading and two needles that can show ADF or VOR information.
notes.explanation: Unlike a movable-card ADF, the pilot does not have to set the heading by hand; a gyrocompass turns the card.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 9 “Navigation Systems”, “Radio Magnetic Indicator (RMI)”, PDF p. 247
notes.evidence: The RMI has two needles, which can be used to indicate navigation information from either the ADF or the VOR receiver.
notes.example: Like a compass rose with two arrows that each point at a different radio mast as you fly past.

notes.front: What is a flight director?
notes.back: A system whose computer blends navigation, air data and attitude inputs into a single steering cue on the attitude display for the pilot to follow.
notes.explanation: The computer processes information from the navigation systems, the ADC and the AHRS, and gives the pilot one cue instead of many readings.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Flight Director System (FDS)”, PDF p. 119
notes.evidence: receives information from the navigation systems, the ADC, AHRS, and other sources of data. The computer processes this
notes.example: Like a sat-nav arrow saying “turn left now”, but for pitch and bank as well as direction.

notes.front: What is a flight management system (FMS)?
notes.back: A master computer linked to all the aircraft’s navigation sensors, controlled from one unit, that builds and flies a flight plan from a navigation database.
notes.explanation: One control point for all sensors replaced separate panels, and a stored database removed the need to type in latitude and longitude for each waypoint.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Flight Management Systems (FMS)”, PDF p. 121
notes.evidence: The concept employed a master computer interfaced with all of the navigation sensors on the aircraft.
notes.example: Like a trip planner that knows every road and junction in the country: you enter the destinations and it strings the route together.

notes.front: With the alternate static source selected, the altimeter reads slightly {{c1::higher}} than the actual altitude.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists this first among the indications to expect when alternate static pressure is used.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Pitot/Static Systems”, PDF p. 98
notes.evidence: When the alternate static source pressure is used, the following instrument indications are observed: 1. The altimeter indicates a slightly higher altitude than

notes.front: The pitot tube’s ram-air opening ices over but its drain hole stays open. What does the airspeed indicator do?
notes.back: The indicated airspeed slowly drops to zero.
notes.explanation: With the drain open, pressure equalises on both sides of the airspeed indicator’s diaphragm, so it no longer senses ram pressure.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Pitot/Static Systems”, PDF p. 98
notes.evidence: indicated airspeed slowly drops to zero.

notes.front: If both the pitot ram-air opening and the drain hole are blocked, the airspeed indicator behaves like which other instrument?
notes.back: An altimeter: indicated airspeed rises in a climb and falls in a descent.
notes.explanation: The handbook gives this as the result when both the ram-air opening and the drain hole are obstructed.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Pitot/Static Systems”, PDF p. 98
notes.evidence: operates like an altimeter as the aircraft climbs and descends.

notes.front: Climbing through cloud with pitot heat off, you see the airspeed rising steadily while pitch and power are unchanged. What is the most likely cause?
notes.back: B: the pitot inlet and drain hole are both blocked.
notes.choices:
A) Static port blocked below your present altitude
B) Pitot ram inlet and drain hole both blocked
C) Alternate static source in use
notes.choicesExplained: A: a static blockage makes the airspeed read low in a climb, not high. C: the alternate source gives a small, steady high reading, not one that keeps rising in a climb.
notes.explanation: With both pitot openings blocked the airspeed indicator acts like an altimeter, so it shows more speed as the aircraft climbs.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Pitot/Static Systems”, PDF p. 98
notes.evidence: operates like an altimeter as the aircraft climbs and descends.

notes.front: The static ports block, and you then climb above that altitude. Does the airspeed indicator read high or low?
notes.back: Low: lower than the actual airspeed.
notes.explanation: The trapped static pressure is higher than normal for the new altitude, which reduces the difference the instrument measures.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Pitot/Static Systems”, PDF p. 98
notes.evidence: than the actual airspeed because the trapped static pressure is higher than normal for that altitude.

notes.front: After a static blockage, you descend below the altitude where it happened. Does the airspeed indicator read high or low?
notes.back: High: faster than the actual airspeed.
notes.explanation: The handbook says the opposite of the climbing case holds, because relatively low static pressure is trapped in the system.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Pitot/Static Systems”, PDF p. 98
notes.evidence: true for operations at lower altitudes; a faster than actual

notes.front: Your static ports froze over at 6,000 feet. You are now descending to 3,000 feet for an approach. Which airspeed indication should you expect?
notes.back: B: higher than your actual airspeed.
notes.choices:
A) Lower than your actual airspeed
B) Higher than your actual airspeed
C) Zero
notes.choicesExplained: A: a low reading is the climbing case, above the blockage altitude. C: a reading that falls to zero comes from a blocked pitot inlet with an open drain.
notes.explanation: Below the blockage altitude the trapped static pressure is relatively low, so the instrument overstates airspeed.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Pitot/Static Systems”, PDF p. 98
notes.evidence: true for operations at lower altitudes; a faster than actual

notes.front: In icing, you select the alternate static source inside the cabin and hold your altitude. What should the instruments do?
notes.back: A: altimeter and airspeed read a little high, and the VSI briefly shows a climb.
notes.choices:
A) Altimeter a little high, airspeed a little high, VSI briefly shows a climb
B) Altimeter a little low, airspeed a little low, VSI briefly shows a descent
C) No change on any instrument
notes.choicesExplained: B: every indication goes the other way from the handbook’s list. C: the handbook expects small changes on all three instruments.
notes.explanation: Knowing the expected changes lets the pilot tell a normal switch-over from a new fault.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Pitot/Static Systems”, PDF p. 98
notes.evidence: actual. 2. The ASI indicates an airspeed greater than the actual airspeed. 3. The VSI shows a momentary climb and then stabilizes if the altitude is held constant.

notes.front: In air colder than standard, true altitude is {{c1::lower}} than the altimeter’s indicated altitude.
notes.explanation: Cold air is denser, so the pressure levels sit closer together and the aircraft is lower than the altimeter suggests.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Cold Weather Altimeter Errors”, PDF p. 100
notes.evidence: of 5,000 feet, its true altitude is lower than it would be if the

notes.front: If you or the FMS apply a cold-temperature correction to an assigned altitude, whom must you tell?
notes.back: ATC: the aircraft is no longer flying the assigned altitude.
notes.explanation: The handbook warns that otherwise vertical separation from other aircraft may be reduced.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Cold Weather Altimeter Errors”, PDF p. 100
notes.evidence: applied by the FMS or manually, ATC must be informed

notes.front: On a −25 °C winter day you cross a fix at the charted minimum altitude with the correct altimeter setting set. How does your real height compare with the chart?
notes.back: B: lower than indicated, so clearance is reduced.
notes.choices:
A) Higher than the altimeter shows
B) Lower than the altimeter shows, so terrain clearance is reduced
C) Exactly as shown, because the altimeter setting is correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is the warm-air case. C: a correct altimeter setting fixes pressure errors, not temperature errors.
notes.explanation: Temperature below standard puts true altitude below indicated altitude, which matters most near terrain and obstacles.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Cold Weather Altimeter Errors”, PDF p. 100
notes.evidence: ISA and true altitude being lower than indicated

notes.front: What type of altitude does a radar altimeter show, and when is it mainly used?
notes.back: Absolute altitude (height above the terrain), mainly during approach and landing.
notes.explanation: It times a signal bounced off the ground, so it measures height above the terrain below rather than pressure altitude.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, PDF p. 124
notes.evidence: Its primary application is to provide accurate absolute altitude

notes.front: In a rate instrument such as a turn coordinator, the gyro precesses in proportion to what?
notes.back: The rate at which the aircraft rotates about one or more of its axes.
notes.explanation: Rate indicators such as turn indicators and turn coordinators work this way; attitude and heading indicators rely on rigidity instead.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Gyroscopic Systems”, PDF p. 111
notes.evidence: rolls over) proportionate to the rate the aircraft rotates about one or more of its axes.

notes.front: Which gyro property do the attitude and heading indicators rely on: rigidity or precession?
notes.back: Rigidity: the gyro stays rigid in its case and the aircraft rotates about it.
notes.explanation: Rate instruments such as turn indicators and turn coordinators use precession instead.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Gyroscopic Systems”, PDF p. 111
notes.evidence: of rigidity. For these instruments, the gyro remains rigid

notes.front: What can stop venturi-driven gyro instruments in flight?
notes.back: Ice clogging the venturi tube.
notes.explanation: The handbook notes that this can stop the instruments when they are most needed.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Gyroscopic Systems”, PDF p. 112
notes.evidence: ice can clog the venturi tube and stop the instruments when

notes.front: Your trainer has a vacuum attitude indicator and heading indicator and an electric turn coordinator. The vacuum pump fails in cloud. Which of these gyro instruments can you still trust?
notes.back: B: the electric turn coordinator.
notes.choices:
A) The attitude indicator
B) The turn coordinator
C) The heading indicator
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: both are driven by the failed vacuum system, so their indications will become unreliable.
notes.explanation: Mixing vacuum and electric gyros is the redundancy the handbook describes: one failure leaves a working rate instrument.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Gyroscopic Systems”, PDF p. 112
notes.evidence: indicators use electric rate indicators and/or the reverse.

notes.front: Why should you check the POH for the power source of each flight instrument?
notes.back: To know what action to take if an instrument fails.
notes.explanation: Some instruments show their power source on the dial, but the handbook says to confirm all of them in the POH.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Gyroscopic Systems”, PDF p. 114
notes.evidence: determine the power source of all instruments to know what

notes.front: During a rapid acceleration, a vacuum attitude indicator may show a slight {{c1::nose-up}} indication.
notes.explanation: The error depends on how fast the erection system works; it is small and corrects itself.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Gyroscopic Instruments”, PDF p. 114
notes.evidence: there may be a slight nose-up indication during a rapid

notes.front: After a {{c1::180°}} turn, an attitude indicator may show a small bank and pitch error.
notes.explanation: These inherent errors are small and correct themselves after straight-and-level flight resumes.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Gyroscopic Instruments”, PDF p. 114
notes.evidence: and pitch error after a 180° turn. These inherent errors are

notes.front: On an instrument take-off roll the attitude indicator shows a slight nose-up pitch before you rotate. What is the best interpretation?
notes.back: C: a normal small acceleration error.
notes.choices:
A) A vacuum failure: cover the instrument
B) The aircraft is already climbing
C) A normal small acceleration error that corrects itself
notes.choicesExplained: A: a slight nose-up during rapid acceleration is an expected error, not a failure sign on its own. B: the aircraft has not rotated, so it is not climbing.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists a slight nose-up indication in rapid acceleration among the attitude indicator’s inherent errors.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Gyroscopic Instruments”, PDF p. 114
notes.evidence: there may be a slight nose-up indication during a rapid

notes.front: Why must a non-slaved gyro heading indicator be set by reference to the magnetic compass?
notes.back: It is not north-seeking.
notes.explanation: Rigidity then holds the heading it was set to, without the compass’s oscillation and errors.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Gyroscopic Instruments”, PDF p. 115
notes.evidence: gyro indicators, are not north seeking, therefore they must

notes.front: A non-slaved heading indicator should be checked against the magnetic compass about every {{c1::15 minutes}}.
notes.explanation: Rigidity holds the heading it was set to, but the handbook still calls for a regular check that it agrees with the compass.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Gyroscopic Instruments”, PDF p. 115
notes.evidence: instrument should be checked about every 15 minutes to see

notes.front: Twenty minutes into level cruise, the (non-slaved) heading indicator reads 267° while the steady magnetic compass reads 275°. What do you do?
notes.back: B: reset the heading indicator to the compass.
notes.choices:
A) Trust the heading indicator; the compass is always less accurate
B) Reset the heading indicator to the compass heading in straight, unaccelerated flight
C) Turn until the two agree
notes.choicesExplained: A: the gyro is not north-seeking and drifts, so it must be matched to the compass. C: turning does not remove the gyro’s error.
notes.explanation: A gyro heading indicator is set by referring to the magnetic compass, and the check is due about every 15 minutes.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Gyroscopic Instruments”, PDF p. 115
notes.evidence: instrument should be checked about every 15 minutes to see

notes.front: A turn coordinator’s gyro gimbal is angled upward about {{c1::30°}} from the aircraft’s longitudinal axis.
notes.explanation: The cant is what lets one rate gyro sense roll as well as yaw.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Gyroscopic Instruments”, PDF p. 116
notes.evidence: turn indicator, but its gimbals frame is angled upward about 30° from the longitudinal axis of the aircraft.

notes.front: On entry to a turn, what does a turn coordinator show first, and what once the turn is stable?
notes.back: First the rate of roll (banking); then, once stabilised, the rate of turn.
notes.explanation: Because it senses both roll and yaw, it responds as soon as the wings start to bank.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Gyroscopic Instruments”, PDF p. 116
notes.evidence: a turn, the indicator first shows the rate of banking and once

notes.front: Does a turn coordinator give any pitch information?
notes.back: No: it does not sense pitch.
notes.explanation: Some dials say so in words, which stops pilots reading the miniature aircraft as a pitch display.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Gyroscopic Instruments”, PDF p. 117
notes.evidence: A turn coordinator does not sense pitch.

notes.front: In level flight you roll into a bank and the turn coordinator’s miniature aircraft moves before the heading has started to change. Is it faulty?
notes.back: A: no, it senses roll rate as well as yaw.
notes.choices:
A) No: it senses roll rate as well as yaw
B) Yes: it should move only once the heading changes
C) Yes: it is showing a pitch change
notes.choicesExplained: B: that describes the turn-and-slip needle, which senses yaw only. C: a turn coordinator does not sense pitch.
notes.explanation: The handbook says the turn coordinator shows the rolling motion even when no turn is yet being made.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 7 “Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers”, “Turn Coordinator”, PDF p. 168
notes.evidence: The turn coordinator’s indicator will indicate the rolling motion although there is no turn being made.

notes.front: In a turn with too much bank for the rate of turn, which way does the inclinometer ball roll?
notes.back: Down to the inside of the turn.
notes.explanation: Gravity then outweighs the inertia of the turn.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Gyroscopic Instruments”, PDF p. 115
notes.evidence: and the ball rolls down to the inside of the turn. If the turn is

notes.front: In a turn with too little bank for the rate of turn, which way does the inclinometer ball roll?
notes.back: Upward to the outside of the turn.
notes.explanation: The inertia of the turn is then greater than gravity.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Gyroscopic Instruments”, PDF p. 116
notes.evidence: made with too shallow a bank angle, the inertia is greater than gravity and the ball rolls upward to the outside of the turn.

notes.front: Does the inclinometer show the amount of bank?
notes.back: No: it only shows the relationship between the angle of bank and the rate of yaw.
notes.explanation: It compares bank with rate of yaw rather than measuring either one.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Gyroscopic Instruments”, PDF p. 116
notes.evidence: The inclinometer does not indicate the amount of bank, nor does it indicate slip; it only indicates the relationship between the angle of bank and the rate of yaw.

notes.front: In a left turn, the inclinometer ball sits to the right of centre, toward the outside of the turn. What is the bank doing relative to the rate of turn?
notes.back: C: too shallow for the rate of turn.
notes.choices:
A) Too steep for the rate of turn
B) Correct for the rate of turn
C) Too shallow for the rate of turn
notes.choicesExplained: A: too steep a bank lets the ball fall to the inside. B: in a coordinated turn the ball stays centred.
notes.explanation: The ball moves to the outside when the inertia of the turn beats gravity, which happens with too little bank.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Gyroscopic Instruments”, PDF p. 116
notes.evidence: made with too shallow a bank angle, the inertia is greater than gravity and the ball rolls upward to the outside of the turn.

notes.front: What have AHRS units replaced, and with what benefit?
notes.back: Traditional gyroscopic flight instruments; they are more reliable, which reduces cost and maintenance.
notes.explanation: The handbook credits AHRS with improved reliability, and so with lower cost and maintenance.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Flight Support Systems”, PDF p. 117
notes.evidence: been replaced by Attitude and Heading Reference Systems (AHRS) improving reliability and thereby reducing cost and

notes.front: On a glass display, which unit supplies the altitude and airspeed, and which the attitude and heading: the AHRS or the ADC?
notes.back: The ADC supplies altitude and airspeed; the AHRS supplies attitude and heading.
notes.explanation: The ADC works from pitot pressure, static pressure and temperature, while the AHRS uses inertial sensors, rate gyros and magnetometers.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Air Data Computer (ADC)”, PDF p. 118
notes.evidence: pressure, and temperature to calculate very precise altitude, IAS, TAS, and air temperature.

notes.front: If the AHRS or the magnetometer fails, which instrument gives you heading?
notes.back: The magnetic compass.
notes.explanation: It needs no other source of power, so it still works when the glass heading source is lost.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 7 “Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers Using an Electronic Flight Display”, “Timed Turns”, PDF p. 214

notes.front: What does a primary flight display replace?
notes.back: The traditional six flight instruments, in one easy-to-scan display.
notes.explanation: Horizon, airspeed, altitude, vertical speed, trend, trim and rate of turn all share one screen.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Electronic Flight Instrument Systems”, PDF p. 122

notes.back: A: the PFD.
notes.choices:
A) The PFD
B) The electronic flight bag
C) The MFD
notes.choicesExplained: C: the MFD shows information in addition to the primary flight information, such as maps. B: an EFB carries charts and documents, not the primary flight instruments.
notes.explanation: The PFD replaces the six traditional flight instruments in one display.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Electronic Flight Instrument Systems”, PDF p. 122

notes.back: A moving map; approach charts (among others).

notes.back: Where airspeed will be after a set time if the current rate continues: 6 seconds on some displays, 10 on others.
notes.explanation: The time depends on the manufacturer; the handbook gives 6 seconds for one light-aircraft system and 10 for an airliner.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying”, “Trend Indicators”, PDF p. 159

notes.front: What are two moments when PFD trend indicators are especially useful?
notes.back: Levelling off at an altitude; rolling out on a heading (or stabilising airspeed).
notes.explanation: The handbook lists these three uses, and adds that trend indicators are not the only tools for holding the desired values.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying”, “Trend Indicators”, PDF p. 160
notes.evidence: Trend indicators are very useful when leveling off at a specific altitude, when rolling out on a heading, or when stabilizing airspeed.

notes.front: On an HSI, the TO/FROM triangle points to the head of the course arrow. What does that tell you?
notes.back: The selected course, properly intercepted and flown, takes the aircraft to the selected facility.
notes.explanation: If it points to the tail instead, the course takes the aircraft directly away from the facility.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Horizontal Situation Indicator (HSI)”, PDF p. 118
notes.evidence: intercepted and flown, takes the aircraft to the selected facility.

notes.front: On an HSI, the glideslope pointer sits below the centre position. Where is the aircraft, and what is needed?
notes.back: Above the glideslope; an increased rate of descent is needed.
notes.explanation: The glideslope deviation pointer shows the aircraft’s position relative to the glideslope.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Horizontal Situation Indicator (HSI)”, PDF p. 118
notes.evidence: center position, the aircraft is above the glideslope, and an increased rate of

notes.front: When must an HSI’s heading be checked against the magnetic compass and reset?
notes.back: In the few installations with no fluxgate, or in emergency operation.
notes.explanation: In most installations the HSI’s azimuth card is a remote indicating compass driven by a fluxgate.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Horizontal Situation Indicator (HSI)”, PDF p. 118
notes.evidence: a fluxgate; however, in few installations where a fluxgate is not installed, or in emergency operation, the heading must

notes.front: You are tracking inbound to a VOR on an HSI with the course set to 040°. The TO/FROM triangle points to the tail of the course arrow. What does this show?
notes.back: A: the course set would take you away from the station.
notes.choices:
A) The course set would take you directly away from the station
B) You are on course to the station
C) You are above the glideslope
notes.choicesExplained: B: a triangle at the head of the arrow would show the course leading to the station. C: the glideslope is shown by a separate pointer.
notes.explanation: The triangle at the tail means the selected course leads away from the facility, so the setting does not match an inbound track.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Horizontal Situation Indicator (HSI)”, PDF p. 118
notes.evidence: flown, takes the aircraft directly away from the selected facility.

notes.front: When an RMI needle is driven by the ADF, what does its head show?
notes.back: The magnetic bearing to the station.
notes.explanation: A gyrocompass turns the RMI’s card to show heading, unlike a movable-card ADF.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 9 “Navigation Systems”, “Radio Magnetic Indicator (RMI)”, PDF p. 247
notes.evidence: When a needle is being driven by the ADF, the head of the needle indicates the MB TO the station tuned on the ADF receiver.

notes.front: If the HSI fails, why is the magnetic compass more likely a supporting instrument than a primary one?
notes.back: Its movements are erratic and unstable.
notes.explanation: It still gives heading, but its swings make it hard to fly precisely by it alone.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 7 “Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers Using an Electronic Flight Display”, “Horizontal Situation Indicator (HSI)”, PDF p. 199
notes.evidence: The magnetic compass can be used as a backup instrument in case of an HSI failure; however, due to erratic, unstable movements,

notes.front: Does a flight director in use mean the autopilot is flying the aircraft?
notes.back: No: it gives steering commands that the pilot follows, or the autopilot follows if coupled.
notes.explanation: The cue is only guidance; someone still has to fly it.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Flight Director System (FDS)”, PDF p. 119
notes.evidence: It should be noted that a flight director in use does not infer the aircraft is being manipulated by the autopilot (coupled), but is providing steering commands that the pilot (or the autopilot, if coupled) follows.

notes.front: With the autopilot off, the flight director command bars move to the left of the aircraft symbol. What should happen?
notes.back: C: the pilot banks left to follow the command.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: the flight director will turn the aircraft
B) The pilot disengages the flight director
C) The pilot banks left to put the symbol back on the command bars
notes.choicesExplained: A: an uncoupled flight director only displays commands; it does not move the controls. B: nothing is wrong; the bars are giving a steering command.
notes.explanation: A flight director provides steering commands for the pilot, or a coupled autopilot, to follow.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Flight Director System (FDS)”, PDF p. 119
notes.evidence: It should be noted that a flight director in use does not infer the aircraft is being manipulated by the autopilot (coupled), but is providing steering commands that the pilot (or the autopilot, if coupled) follows.

notes.front: Which flight director/autopilot mode follows the heading the pilot selects?
notes.back: Heading mode.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists it with the VOR/localiser and approach modes among those a pilot may choose.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Flight Director System (FDS)”, PDF p. 119
notes.evidence: the HDG (heading) mode, the VOR/LOC (localizer tracking)

notes.front: Which flight director/autopilot mode tracks a VOR radial or a localiser course?
notes.back: The VOR/localiser (navigation) tracking mode.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls it the localiser tracking mode.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Flight Director System (FDS)”, PDF p. 119
notes.evidence: the HDG (heading) mode, the VOR/LOC (localizer tracking)

notes.front: Which flight director/autopilot mode captures and tracks both the ILS localiser and the glidepath?
notes.back: Approach (glideslope) mode.
notes.explanation: It adds vertical tracking to the lateral tracking of the navigation mode.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Flight Director System (FDS)”, PDF p. 119
notes.evidence: tracking of instrument landing system (ILS) localizers and glidepath) mode.

notes.front: ATC vectors you to intercept the ILS and you want the autopilot to capture the localiser and then the glidepath on its own. Which mode do you arm?
notes.back: A: approach mode.
notes.choices:
A) Approach mode
B) VOR/localiser mode alone
C) Heading mode
notes.choicesExplained: C: heading mode only holds the selected heading. B: navigation mode tracks the localiser course but not the glidepath.
notes.explanation: Approach mode is the one the handbook describes as capturing and tracking both the localiser and the glidepath.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Flight Director System (FDS)”, PDF p. 119
notes.evidence: tracking of instrument landing system (ILS) localizers and glidepath) mode.

notes.front: Electronic navigation databases, such as an FMS uses, are updated every {{c1::28 days}}.
notes.explanation: The Aeronautical Information Manual likewise requires current databases for IFR GPS operations.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Electronic Flight Instrument Systems”, PDF p. 122
notes.evidence: electronic navigation databases are updated every 28 days.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An FMS without GPS computes its position from distances to several DME stations it picks from its database. How good can that position be?
notes.back: C: nearly as accurate as GPS.
notes.choices:
A) Unusable without a VOR
B) Only good enough for VFR
C) Nearly as accurate as GPS
notes.choicesExplained: B: the handbook puts multi-DME accuracy close to GPS. A: the FMS uses the distances alone, correcting for aircraft and station altitude.
notes.explanation: The FMS corrects for aircraft and station altitude using the database, so the combined distances give a precise fix.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Electronic Flight Instrument Systems”, PDF p. 122
notes.evidence: FMS can compute a position nearly as accurately as GPS.

notes.front: What are two functions an electronic flight bag can provide?
notes.back: Aeronautical charts; checklists (among others).
notes.explanation: The handbook’s list is open: it also names documents, weight and balance, fuel calculations, moving maps and logbooks.
notes.source: Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), ch. 5 “Improvement Plans”, “Electronic Flight Bag (EFB)”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: Functions include, but are not limited to, aeronautical charts, documents, checklists, weight & balance, fuel calculations, moving maps, and logbooks.

notes.front: When is a portable device (such as a tablet) considered an EFB?
notes.back: Only when it hosts and actively displays Type A or Type B EFB software applications.
notes.explanation: The hardware alone is just a portable electronic device; the approved applications make it an EFB.
notes.source: Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), ch. 5 “Improvement Plans”, “Electronic Flight Bag (EFB)”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: hardware device hosts and actively displays either Type A or B software application(s).

notes.front: What integrity alerting do VFR panel-mount and hand-held GPS receivers lack?
notes.back: RAIM alerting: they cannot warn of too few satellites or a position error.
notes.explanation: The manual therefore tells pilots to cross-check such units against other navigation.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-17 “Global Positioning System (GPS)”
notes.evidence: VFR GPS panel mount receivers and hand-held units have no RAIM alerting capability.

notes.front: GPS navigation databases {{c1::must}} be updated for IFR operations and should be updated for all other operations.
notes.explanation: The manual draws the line: current data is required for IFR, recommended otherwise.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-17 “Global Positioning System (GPS)”
notes.evidence: Databases must be updated for IFR operations and should be updated for all other operations.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In cloud, your only VOR receiver fails. Your tablet with a GPS moving map still shows your position. May you use it to fly an instrument approach?
notes.back: A: no, hand-held GPS is not authorised for approaches.
notes.choices:
A) No: hand-held GPS is not authorised for instrument approaches
B) Yes, if the tablet’s database is current
C) Yes, if ATC approves
notes.choicesExplained: B: a current database does not make a hand-held unit approved IFR equipment. C: ATC cannot turn a hand-held unit into approved IFR equipment.
notes.explanation: The manual rules out VFR and hand-held GPS for IFR navigation, approaches and as a principal flight reference.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, ch. 1 sec. 1, para 1-1-17 “Global Positioning System (GPS)”
notes.evidence: Visual flight rules (VFR) and hand-held GPS systems are not authorized for IFR navigation, instrument approaches, or as a principal instrument flight reference.
